name: Elena Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for agreeing to talk. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say gets your name on it. Could you describe a normal day at work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do policy admin for home insurance at Northfield Home Cover, in a grey office on a business park by the ring road. Most of my day is changes: someone moves house, adds a conservatory, wants a bike covered, and I update the policy and send the new documents. Renewals in the afternoon, mainly people ringing up cross about their price going up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same each day. I've got my checklist taped to the bottom of my screen and I go through it in order. What gets to me is when they change the system, which they've done twice since I started, and everyone says it's easier and I'm the one ringing IT. I switched off that suggested-reply thing as soon as it appeared, it put words in my emails I'd never use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad, honestly. I'd rather things just stayed as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. I don't post online much, but I'd probably say the same to my sister at Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried. Even the small stuff your card mentions, like routine tasks, that's most of my day. If the system starts doing address changes on its own, there's a fair bit less for me to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it and try to be quicker on renewals, since my numbers aren't great. I'd keep the savings where they are, about two months, and not take on anything new. Maybe I'd look at whether Kerem's hours settle down before we think about moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, because I'm still the slow one on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on your mind at home, apart from work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerem, my boyfriend, is a sous-chef, and his restaurant cut a night last month. If they cut another, we'd be on my wage for the rent. That worries me more than computers, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If even a few tasks went, who at Northfield would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the cancellations team. Some people already lost hours there when the online form came in. I'd just hope it doesn't happen to us.

say: I'd tell colleagues it was **all that fuss** for nothing.
I'd say the same to my sister at **Sunday dinner**.
think: The routine tasks AI takes are **most of my day**, so even small changes reach me.
Being **the slow one** on renewals is a worry already.
do: Keep **my checklist** and try to be quicker on renewals.
Hold savings at about **two months** and take on nothing new.
Wait to see if my boyfriend's **restaurant hours** settle before moving.
feel: Mostly okay, a bit **uneasy** about being slow on the team.
S0.quote: Even the small stuff your card mentions, like routine tasks, that's most of my day.
fieldNote: She wants **nothing to change** and turned off AI tools on sight.
Her real household pressure is her boyfriend's **shrinking restaurant hours**.
She already saw the **cancellations team** lose hours to an online form.

steps.text: Keep working through her taped renewal checklist each afternoon
Hold off on moving until her boyfriend's restaurant shifts settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd hate. That's my job written down on your card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it quiet at work, mostly. I'd say something like, well, they'll still need someone who knows the policies. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just read what other people said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be one of the first to go. I'm junior, I'm not fast, I don't use the AI stuff, and policy changes are exactly the kind of checking and writing it says. I'd see the redundancy letter coming a mile off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday this summer, cancel the gym I don't go to, stop the takeaways. I'd look at jobs that aren't on a computer all day, maybe in the council's housing office, where you meet people face to face. I'd ask my uncle about his flooring business too, but only if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like waiting for a phone call you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've switched off the AI tools so far. Wouldn't learning them help you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I know. Everyone says that. I'd be learning AI just to train my own replacement, and then I'd still be the junior who learned it late. I'd rather spend the energy finding something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It's not the machine I'm cross with. It's that the company calls it efficiency, and it means me.

say: I'd say quietly that they'll **still need someone** who knows the policies.
I wouldn't post anything, just **read what others** say.
think: I'd be **one of the first** to go: junior, slow, no AI.
Learning the tools would just mean **training my replacement**.
do: Cancel the **gym and takeaways** and skip this summer's holiday.
Apply for **face-to-face jobs**, like the council housing office.
Ask my **uncle's flooring business** for work only if needed.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a phone call you know is coming.
S1.quote: I'd be learning AI just to train my own replacement, and then I'd still be the junior who learned it late.
fieldNote: She expects a **redundancy letter** and sees herself first in line.
She **refuses to learn AI**, which she frames as pointless rather than scary.
Her blame lands on the **company's word efficiency**, not the technology.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and stop takeaways, skip the summer holiday
Apply for face-to-face jobs like the council housing office
Ask her uncle about work in his flooring business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. That's not fair on anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone would be saying: it's too fast, somebody should have stopped it. I'd be one of those people nodding along at work and not doing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at Northfield, probably inside a year. There's nothing in my job that isn't a screen. The only thing that would be left of me at Northfield is my mug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my uncle first and ask about the flooring work properly, carrying, cutting, fitting, whatever he needs. I'd stop saving for anything and just make the two months last. We'd probably move in with my mum to save rent, which Kerem would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I can't breathe properly. I'd be awake every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says hands-on robots come about three years later. What does that mean for you and your boyfriend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerem's in a kitchen, so he'd have a few more years before robots come, if your card's right. That's what we'd live on. But a sous-chef wage on its own doesn't cover our rent, so it'd be my mum's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't like change. How would you handle starting something completely new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably just do it, if it's that or nothing. I wouldn't like it. I'd hate it, actually. But laying floors is a real job a computer can't do yet.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone should have stopped it.
I'd **nod along** at work without doing much.
think: I'd be **finished at Northfield** within a year; nothing in my job is off-screen.
My boyfriend's **kitchen job** gives us a few extra years, not enough for rent.
do: Ask my **uncle** for proper flooring work, carrying and fitting.
Move into **my mum's** spare room to save rent.
Make the **two months** of savings last as long as possible.
feel: Like I **can't breathe**, awake every night.
S2.quote: There's nothing in my job that isn't a screen. The only thing that would be left of me at Northfield is my mug.
fieldNote: She jumps straight to **family support**: uncle's business and her mum's spare room.
She'd accept **hands-on work** she dislikes because it's further from the machines.
Her plan is **survival**, not ambition, and she says so.

steps.text: Ask her uncle for flooring work, carrying and fitting
Move into her mum's spare room to save rent
Stop spending on anything beyond rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. I'd still hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we've got time, let's not panic. I'd say it because everybody would be saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just later. I'd still lose the job. Five years of warning just means I'd spend five years watching my job at Northfield get closer to the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see who goes first at Northfield. Then I'd do something, probably the council job if it's still there, or a course in something practical. I'd build the savings up a bit more, maybe to four months, because there'd be time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time. Like a dentist appointment that's five years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year or two. Isn't that time you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. I know that's what I'd do, though. I'm not someone who jumps first. I'd watch Jodie and the others and go when they go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be good at, outside insurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably maths and practical stuff. I left school with decent grades. Something like a plumbing course, maybe, though I've never even changed a tap.

say: I'd say **we've got time**, let's not panic, because everyone would.
I'd keep my **real worry** to myself at work.
think: It's the **same ending**, just later; I'd still lose the job.
Extra time means **watching it get closer** for five years.
do: Wait **a year or two** to see who goes first at Northfield.
Then apply to the **council job** or a practical course.
feel: **Uneasy** all the time, like a far-off dentist appointment.
S3.quote: Five years of warning just means I'd spend five years watching my job at Northfield get closer to the door.
fieldNote: She'd **wait for others** to move, which matches her resistance to change.
The extra time brings **more savings**, but not more willingness to act.
Her mood stays high because she **still expects** to lose the job.

steps.text: Watch who Northfield lets go first before deciding anything
Build savings up to four months of rent and bills
Apply for the council housing office job after that

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd probably say it'll never happen, and I'd half believe it. Ten years ago nobody had a smartphone that did half of what they do now, and we're still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd have to learn the AI things at some point in those ten years, even if I hate it, because the others would be using them and I'd stick out. I'd do the minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and do whatever training Northfield makes compulsory, nothing extra. I'd save steadily, and maybe Kerem and I would get married in that time, which I'd want to do before things change. If the council job came up, I'd go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Less frightened, but it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a wedding. Would the timing change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the wedding before thirty, I think. Ten years gives us time, and I'd rather do it while we've both got steady jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you start worrying properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years later, if I'm still at Northfield. Then I'd be really worried. But I'd still have time to get out before it hits.

say: I'd say at work it'll **never happen**, and half believe it.
I'd point out how much changed **in ten years** before and we're still here.
think: I'd have to learn the **AI tools** at some point, even if I hate it.
I'd still have **time to get out** before it hits.
do: Do only the **compulsory training** Northfield sets.
Save steadily and plan **the wedding** with my boyfriend before thirty.
Apply for the **council job** if it comes up.
feel: **Uneasy**, less frightened, but it's still there.
S4.quote: I'd have to learn the AI things at some point in those ten years, even if I hate it, because the others would be using them and I'd stick out.
fieldNote: With a decade, she grudgingly accepts **learning AI**, but only the minimum.
**Wedding plans** come forward to lock in stability while jobs feel steady.
She stays **anxious** because her job still looks likely to go by the end.

steps.text: Do only the AI training Northfield makes compulsory
Plan the wedding with her boyfriend before thirty
Put a fixed amount into savings every payday

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for anything except panic. What would help is if companies had to keep people on for a while, or give real notice and pay for a course. I'm not good at finding new things on my own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people want this. Nobody asked me if I wanted AI in my office. I'd like someone to ask before it happens, not after.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked me if I wanted AI in my office. I'd like someone to ask before it happens, not after.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** home insurance policy admin at Northfield, slow on renewals and attached to her checklist.
She lives with her boyfriend, a **sous-chef** whose hours are being cut, with about two months saved.
She **never uses AI** tools and expects to be among the first let go.
Faced with fast change, she leans on **family**: her uncle's flooring business and her mum's spare room.
With more time she'd **wait and watch** others before moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for anything but panic.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice periods** and company-paid courses, since she struggles to find new paths alone.
